chunks: "You can't measure SoC directly. You estimate it, and there are three basic ways. The first is voltage.
The open-circuit voltage maps to state of charge through a lookup table, so if the cell has rested I can read the voltage and look up SoC.
It's simple and has no drift, but the curve is really flat in the middle, only about 6 millivolts per percent, so a 10 millivolts measurement error is already a couple of percent.
And under load the voltage sags by I R , so it's useless while the device is running unless I correct for it.
The second is coulomb counting: integrate the current in and out and subtract from the full capacity.
That works under load and is smooth, but any offset in the current sensor integrates into a drift. A 10 milliamp offset on a 2 amp-hour cell is 12 percent per day.
And it needs a known starting point and the correct capacity, which falls with age and temperature.

So real fuel gauges combine them: coulomb counting for short-term tracking, with voltage corrections whenever the cell is at rest or at the full and empty endpoints, often through a Kalman filter or an impedance-tracking model that also learns capacity and resistance over time.
Why it's hard overall: flat curve, load and temperature dependence, hysteresis, aging, sensor error, and the fact that the thing you are estimating, the full capacity, itself moves."
